name: PT Nippon Indosari Corpindo Tbk

frontmatter.title: Nippon Indosari Corpindo: a permanent cost reset, not a trough
frontmatter.summary: Nippon Indosari's cost step-up is not a bad quarter. The expired-inventory charge is structural at a higher share of revenue, wages and route costs inflate against flat volume, and the filings show no operating leverage to give back. At Rp346 we rate the shares REDUCE: the price discounts a margin recovery the record does not support, while the cash flow is real and the balance sheet is manageable.
thesis: Revenue has not grown for four years and the two minimarket chains that take most of the volume are not a growth channel; the story is cost, not top line [S3].

The trough is mostly permanent. The expired-inventory charge runs at a tenth of revenue, the advertising step-up is only assumed back to its FY2025 share, and a flat-volume cost base inflating at the same rate as price leaves no operating leverage to recover [S2][S3].
The deck's wheat path sits well above spot, so gross margin stays below its FY2025 level in every forecast year; the margin reset is an input cost, not a demand problem [S4][S7].

{'Cash generation is better than the profit line suggests': 'FY2026E free cash flow to the firm is IDR287.0bn while the dividend resets to Rp26 per share, and no net new borrowing is needed after this year [S2].'}
Our discounted cash flow gives Rp308 per share and, after the house liquidity schedule's 20% discount, a target of Rp346 and a -22.0% total return, a REDUCE at the current price [S0].
{'The market is not paying for our base case': 'the price implies FY2027E revenue growth of 8.3% against our 3.0% forecast, or else a margin recovery we cannot source [S0].'}

blocks.text: Nippon Indosari Corpindo bakes the Sari Roti range and delivers it, daily, to a distribution footprint that few consumer names in Indonesia can match. We initiate coverage at REDUCE with a twelve-month target of Rp346 against a last price of Rp476, a total return of -22.0% including Rp26 of forecast dividend. The construction is three steps and it is worth stating it exactly: the probability-weighted value across our three methods is Rp432, of which the discounted cash flow contributes Rp308 at a 75% weight; the house liquidity schedule then applies the 20% tier set by traded value, taking the target to Rp346 [S0]. Between fifty and fifty-six rupiah a share of that target is value struck on FY2025A multiples we show but call stale — re-pointed at FY2027E the same blend would put the target near two hundred and ninety rupiah — and we keep it only because the market screens the name on those multiples, not because we defend the earnings base. The discount is not a discretionary haircut: fund rules fixes it off IDR325.7m a day behind a 7.6% public float. We charge illiquidity once, here, and not a second time as a premium in the discount rate.

The cost side, not the demand side, decides the value here. Nine-month operating profit was IDR122.6bn on revenue of IDR2,739.3bn, against a far higher prior-year figure on essentially the same sales [S2 p.6]. The incremental drivers are advertising and promotion, which rose from IDR143.1bn in the first nine months of FY2025 to IDR179.7bn in the same period of FY2026, and a gross-margin give-up of a point and a half as the flour repricing landed ahead of the annual price round [S2 p.6, p.79]. The expired and defective inventory charge of IDR260.6bn is not the year-on-year swing — it rose only from IDR241.4bn — but it is the reason the trough does not normalise away: it is a structural cost of a short-shelf-life route business and the audited FY2025 figure of IDR328.5bn shows the same order of magnitude in a normal year [S3 p.90]. We hold it permanent in the cost base.

The operating leverage the bull case needs is not in the filings. The FY2025 note splits operating expenses: expired and defective inventory, transportation, distribution fees and hawker welfare are forty-two per cent of the line and all four move with volume, which is flat [S3 p.90]; salaries and benefits are a third and grow with minimum wages, with Government Regulation 49/2025 resetting the floor from January 2026 [S4 p.45]; the rest — rent, utilities, repairs, depreciation carried in opex — is fixed and inflates. Weighted at four per cent on salaries, just over three per cent on the volume-linked block and three per cent elsewhere, the line inflates at about the same rate as the price-led revenue path, so the ratio is flat, not falling. That gives a long-run net operating-cost ratio of 43.8% of revenue, marginally above the audited FY2025 net ratio — operating expenses of IDR1,606.9bn on revenue of IDR3,757.6bn, about forty-three per cent of sales, not the data pack's gross line [S3 p.16]. The FY2022A-FY2025A record supports that read: the net ratio rose as revenue stagnated, so the company has demonstrated operating deleverage, not leverage.

The price disagrees, and the disagreement is the thesis. Solving the model for the FY2027E revenue growth that reproduces today's Rp476 gives 8.3% against the 3.0% we forecast [S0]. The cross-checks do not rescue it: on the last audited year the price-to-earnings method gives Rp621 and the EV/EBITDA method Rp803, but those capitalise a year struck before the cost reset; re-pointed at the earnings the market is actually discounting, the shares trade at 17.8x FY2027E earnings and 7.0x FY2027E EBITDA on our forecasts, which is where a mature staple with a damaged margin belongs and which brackets our target rather than contradicting it [S2 p.6]. What would move us up: advertising normalising faster than we assume, wheat retracing from the deck's path toward the much lower spot, and a January price round that sticks. What would move us down: the advertising step-up proving permanent, a further rebate round from the two chains, and a second year of expired-inventory charges near a tenth of revenue. The bull case is worth Rp671 and the bear case Rp242, carried at 25% and 30%.

The depreciation restatement stands and it cuts the other way, which is why the rating is not harsher. The data pack carries a charge about a quarter of the audited one; the FY2025 note charges IDR185.4bn to operations, and on that basis FY2025 EBITDA is IDR572.1bn [S3 p.63]. The business still converts cash: free cash flow to the firm of IDR287.0bn in FY2026E against a market value of IDR2,676,203.1m, net debt of IDR567.5bn and no net new borrowing after this year. That is a real, cash-generative franchise trading above what its evidenced cost structure supports — a REDUCE, not a sell on a broken balance sheet.

Nippon Indosari Corpindo is an industrial bakery, not a craft one: it mixes, proofs, bakes and packs bread in factories and then distributes it through its own fleet to the outlets that sell it the same day. The company operates 15 bakeries spread across Indonesia and its products reach more than 100,000 points of sale [S4 p.112, p.52]. That model — high-volume plants, short shelf life, daily route delivery — is the whole business. It explains why the company reports a single operating segment split geographically rather than by product [S3 p.47], why returns on a stale loaf are an operating cost rather than an exceptional item, and why the distribution network, not the recipe, is the asset that keeps competitors out.

The product architecture has moved beyond the original white loaf. The company now runs six business units — Sari Roti for the core bread range, Sari Kue for cakes, Sari Choco for chocolate-based products, Food Solutions for business-to-business supply, Distribution for the route network, and Retail for its own outlets — and management presents the expansion into new products, new business units and new channels as a deliberate decision to push revenue rather than defend a single category [S4 p.3]. The strategy matters for the forecast because it is the only identifiable source of volume growth in a company whose revenue has been flat since FY2022, and because it is capital-light: nine-month capital expenditure was IDR46.0bn, a run rate consistent with maintenance and route refresh rather than new capacity [S2 p.8].

The customer base is the most important structural fact about the business. PT Indomarco Prismatama, the Indomaret chain, took 34.7% of FY2025 net revenue, and the two largest customers together took 60.0% [S3 p.89]. Both are modern-trade chains with national scale, both are sophisticated buyers of a product with a one-day shelf life, and one of them is a related party. This is simultaneously the company's greatest strength — guaranteed volume, fast rotation, national reach without building its own stores — and its greatest constraint, because a supplier that depends on two buyers for three-fifths of its revenue does not set the terms of trade. The nine-month promotion line is the price of that dependence, and we treat the rebate cycle as a permanent feature of the revenue model rather than a temporary cost.

Ownership is concentrated. PT Indoritel Makmur Internasional holds 25.8%, treasury stock accounts for 564 million shares of the 6,186 million issued, and the public holds 7.6% [S4 p.21]. The annual report's shareholder analysis traces the two largest blocks to the ultimate families behind the listed holding companies, which means control sits with two groups whose interests have historically been aligned with the listed entity but whose other ventures are not part of it. For a minority holder the practical consequences are a thin float, a small free-float weighting in any index, and a governance channel that runs through the controlling groups rather than through the board.

The company employs 5,553 people [S0], a large share of them in distribution rather than manufacturing. That labour model is a moat in one direction — a route network built over decades is expensive to replicate — and a fixed cost in the other, because the vans and drivers run whether or not the volume is there. That is the structural reason the margin travels in one direction when revenue stalls: the same largely fixed footprint that produced an operating margin above ten per cent in FY2024 produced a margin under six per cent in the first nine months of FY2026, and the cost does not come out when the sales do not come in.

The Indonesian packaged-bread category grew out of a simple observation: a tropical country with a rice-based diet still needs cheap, shelf-stable food for the urban commute, and a branded loaf with a printed date is more trustworthy than an unbranded one. The companies that won were those that solved distribution rather than baking — a bakery is easy to build, a daily route to tens of thousands of warungs and minimarkets is not. That is why the category consolidated around a handful of national brands while regional bakeries stayed regional, and why the modern-trade chains that grew fastest became the most important customers of the bakers. It also explains the category's structural weakness: bread is a discretionary purchase at the margin, so volume falls first when household budgets tighten, while the route cost does not.

We do not have an independent, dated market-size estimate for the branded bread category in our archive, and we will not invent one. What the filings support is a description of the demand drivers and a set of cost facts that determine profitability; the company's own view of the category's prospects, stated in the annual report with reference to national growth, is a company view and we treat it as such rather than as evidence [S4 p.51]. Our working assumption is that the category grows with urban population and modern-trade penetration, in the low single digits in volume, and that value growth comes from price. Everything in this report follows from that assumption.

The cost chain is where the industry's economics are decided. Indonesia imports almost all of the wheat it mills and took in roughly eleven and three-quarter million tonnes in 2025, a near-total dependence on imported grain [S7]. Wheat on the Chicago board was down from its August peak in early October 2026 but still up 32.0% year on year [S7], retail Cakra Kembar flour was quoted at Rp11,490/kg per kilogram in the first week of October [S7], and the press discussion since has been about a further milling pass-through whose size Kompas states as a conditional rather than an observed change [S8]. Our sector deck carries the transmission: wheat at US$196/t in FY2025A, US$294/t in FY2026E, US$294/t in FY2027E and US$284/t into the long run, against a spot of US$218/t. We use the deck as given: a cost that stays high through the next eighteen months and only then relaxes toward its through-cycle level.

The other deck input, palm oil, is a minor exposure. Crude palm oil runs at US$1,135/t in our deck, rising to US$1,240/t and settling at US$1,150/t, and it reaches Nippon Indosari only through the margarine and shortening in its recipes, which is why we model it at two per cent of cost of goods sold [S3 p.61]. The rupiah matters more than palm: the deck has the dollar at Rp17,570/USD in FY2026E and Rp18,350/USD in FY2027E, and although flour is bought in rupiah, it is priced off import parity, so a weaker currency is a cost line with a lag. There is no administered price for bread and no subsidy in the chain; the only regulation that touches the business is the import regime for wheat and the food-safety and labelling rules that apply to any packaged food, neither of which we expect to change the economics.

On competition, the structure is a national leader against regional bakeries and unbranded substitutes rather than a fight between equals. Nippon Indosari's advantage is the route network and the shelf presence that comes with it, and the company's own disclosure of the reach of its products is the best evidence we have for that advantage [S4 p.52]. We are explicit about the limit of that evidence: the filings do not disclose a market share, and we have no independent measurement, so we treat leadership as a distribution fact rather than a quantified share. The competitive pressure we can see in the numbers is price: advertising and promotion rose by roughly a quarter year on year in the first nine months of FY2026 while revenue was flat [S2 p.79], which is what defending volume in a mature category looks like.

The five forces, as we see them. Supplier power is high and concentrated: wheat is imported, milling is dominated by one large group, and the baker is a price-taker on both. Buyer power is high and rising: the two chains take 60.0% of revenue [S3 p.89] and negotiate as national accounts. The threat of substitutes is high but stable: rice, noodles and instant food are cheaper calories, and unbranded bread competes on price in the general trade. The threat of new entrants is low at national scale — nobody is going to replicate a daily route to more than 100,000 outlets — but high at the local level, where a single bakery can serve a town. Rivalry is moderate in branding and severe in price at the point of sale, which is exactly what a mature, perishable, capacity-heavy category should look like. The moat is real, it is the distribution network, and it is being taxed by the customers who use it.

Revenue has not grown for four years. Net revenue was IDR3,935.2bn in FY2022A, IDR3,820.5bn in FY2023A, IDR3,932.2bn in FY2024A and IDR3,757.6bn in FY2025A [S3 p.16, F1/F2]. In nominal terms that is a decline, and against cumulative food inflation it is a substantial real contraction in volume: the company has been selling fewer loaves at higher prices for four years. The first nine months of FY2026 continued the pattern, with revenue of IDR2,739.3bn against a marginally higher prior-year figure in the same filing [S2 p.6]. We forecast revenue of IDR3,744.5bn for FY2026E, essentially flat, and then 3.0% in FY2027E and 3.5% a year through FY2030E, which is price at the house inflation path with volume flat to slightly down. That is not a cautious assumption dressed as a forecast; it is what the last four years of actuals support.

The margin history is the part of the model that earns its keep. Gross margin was 53.0% in FY2022A, 54.0% in FY2023A, 54.6% in FY2024A and 53.1% in FY2025A — a range that held through a complete round trip in the wheat price — and it falls to 51.3% in our FY2026E, 50.6% in FY2027E and 50.1% by FY2030E [S3 p.16, S2 p.6]. The company's record supports a high pass-through of a raw-material move at the gross line and a lag of about a year, which is why our forecast shows the margin giving up ground in FY2027E rather than in FY2026E: the flour repricing lands in the fourth quarter of FY2026 and is only partly recovered in the following price round. The remaining part that is not passed through is the promotional element of the price ladder, and it is why the margin does not return to its FY2024A level in any year of our forecast.

Operating costs are where the value is decided, and the filings do not support an operating-leverage recovery. Nine-month operating expenses of IDR1,371.2bn consumed half of revenue, and the three largest moving parts are visible in the notes: expired and defective inventory of IDR260.6bn, advertising and promotion of IDR179.7bn, and transportation of IDR227.1bn [S2 p.79]. The year-on-year increase is concentrated in advertising, which rose from IDR143.1bn in the first nine months of FY2025, and in the gross line; the expiry charge rose only from IDR241.4bn [S2 p.79]. We still treat the expiry charge as permanent rather than as a bad quarter: it is a function of the return and variable-consideration terms the company offers its customers — the filing describes rights of return and price and volume adjustments in its revenue contracts [S3 p.36] — it scales with the difficulty of selling a perishable product through somebody else's shelf space, and the audited FY2025 charge was IDR328.5bn in a year the company would call normal [S3 p.90]. Scrap sales of IDR80.1bn recover part of that cost as other operating income [S2 p.79]; we keep the offset visible rather than netting it silently.

The cost base explains why the trough does not close. On the FY2025 note, expired inventory, transportation, distribution fees and hawker welfare are forty-two per cent of operating expenses and all four move with volume, which is flat; salaries and benefits are a third and grow with minimum wages, with Government Regulation 49/2025 resetting the floor from January 2026 [S3 p.90][S4 p.45]; depreciation carried in opex, rent, utilities, repairs and professional fees are fixed and inflate. Weighted at four per cent on salaries, just over three per cent on the volume-linked block and three per cent elsewhere, the line inflates at about the same rate as the price-led revenue path. Our forecast therefore takes operating expenses from IDR1,686.9bn in FY2026E to IDR1,872.9bn in FY2030E while revenue grows from IDR3,744.5bn to IDR4,276.1bn; the ratio eases from 45.1% to 43.8% only because the advertising step-up is assumed back to its FY2025 share of sales, not because the fixed base absorbs growth [S2 p.79].

The depreciation line needed restating. The data pack carries a FY2025 depreciation and amortisation charge of about a quarter of the audited figure; the audited notes charge IDR185.4bn to operations in FY2025 and IDR177.2bn in FY2024 [S3 p.63]. We have restated both years as facts and the engine rebuilds the history from them, which lifts FY2025 EBITDA to IDR572.1bn and explains why the FY2026E EBITDA of IDR423.1bn carries a much lower margin than the prior year: the revenue base fell, the cost base did not, and the depreciation charge of IDR189.8bn is larger than the capital spending that supports it. The operating-expense line needed the same treatment. The data pack's line is gross of other operating income, which is why gross profit less that line does not foot to the printed operating profit; the LK's net line is operating expenses of IDR1,712.9bn less other operating income of IDR109.1bn plus other operating expense of IDR3.1bn, or IDR1,606.9bn, and the same bridge on FY2024A gives IDR1,625.3bn. We restate both years as facts, so the history foots to operating profit of IDR386.7bn and our FY2025A cost ratio is the audited one. Readers who screen this name on a data-vendor EBITDA will be looking at a business about one and four-tenths times as profitable as it is: the pack's EBITDA understates the audited figure by roughly a quarter.

Cash generation is the strongest part of the story and the reason the rating is REDUCE rather than SELL. Operating cash flow was IDR250.0bn in the first nine months of FY2026 against net profit of IDR54.9bn [S2 p.6, p.8] — a conversion rate several times earnings, driven by the depreciation add-back and by working capital that is structurally light: around three-fifths of sales go to two chains on short terms, and operating working capital runs at about 4.5% of revenue [S3 p.89]. The balance sheet is levered but not stretched. Cash was IDR182.5bn at the end of September against a short-term bank loan of IDR425.0bn [S2 p.4-5], giving net debt of IDR567.5bn for the year and 1.3x of EBITDA on our forecasts, falling to 1.1x in FY2027E. Finance costs of IDR47.6bn in nine months annualise to a rate in the high single digits on the current book, and the facilities are floating [S2 p.6][S4 p.83].

Capital allocation has been generous to shareholders and is now constrained by it. The FY2024 dividend was 99.5% of profit [S4 p.53]; the FY2025 dividend of IDR450.0bn was paid on profit of IDR258.5bn [S2 p.8], which is why gross debt rose over the same period. We model a hundred per cent payout of each year's profit from FY2026E, giving dividends per share of Rp26 and Rp27 in the two forecast years, and no net new borrowing after FY2026E. The announced cancellation of treasury stock is a capital-structure clean-up rather than a per-share event: it retires about 514 million shares against the 564 million held in treasury at the prior year end [S6, F24/F29], which reduces issued capital and treasury stock by the same amount and leaves shares outstanding — the count that matters for earnings per share — where they were.

Earnings quality, on the house screens. The accruals test is the one we can run cleanly only for the current year: nine-month operating cash flow exceeded net profit several times over, which is a negative accrual position, the opposite of the warning sign [S2 p.8]. We have not computed a full three-year Sloan ratio because the archived filing set for this initiation covers two fiscal years and the earlier cash-flow statements were not part of it — a gap in our evidence, stated rather than papered over. The divergence tests are clean: related-party trade receivables fell from a higher base to IDR200.2bn at the end of September [S2 p.4], so receivables are not outgrowing revenue; there is no capitalised development cost in this business to hide a cost on the balance sheet; and the inventory build that matters is charged through the income statement every quarter rather than stored. The one genuine quality flag is the expiry charge itself: a cost that recurs at close to a tenth of revenue is an operating reality of the route model, not an accounting accident, and it should be treated as permanent rather than as a bad quarter. On the IDX regime screens we found no special notation letter or monitoring-board status in the filings we archived, and the FY2025 consolidated statements carry an unqualified audit opinion [S3 p.4]. The structural flags are the thin float of 7.6% and the treasury-stock history, both of which we price through the liquidity discount rather than through the earnings model [S4 p.21].

The method set follows the industry card for compounder-quality consumer names. This is an asset-backed, mature, cash-generative business with a visible cost structure and a dividend policy, so a discounted cash flow is the primary method, carrying 75% of the weight. We keep two multiples as cross-checks because the market prices this name on earnings and on EBITDA, and a report that ignores the multiples the market actually uses is not useful to a portfolio manager. The weights are 15% for the price-to-earnings cross-check and 10% for EV/EBITDA.

The cost of capital is stated honestly because the house band is not met on the blended rate. The risk-free rate is 7.4% after the sovereign default spread of 1.6%, the mature-market equity risk premium is 4.2% and the Indonesia country premium is 2.5%; with an unlevered beta of 0.70 — the house consumer-staples default, since the pack carries no index series from which to fit a measured beta — and gearing of 0.33 the levered beta is 0.88. We add no float premium: the 7.6% public float is charged once, through the liquidity-discount schedule, and a second charge in the discount rate would double-count the same illiquidity. The cost of equity is 11.7%, inside the eleven to thirteen per cent band the house requires for rupiah names. Pre-tax cost of debt in the discount rate is 9.4% on the 22.0% statutory tax shield, the weights are 75% equity and 25% debt, and the blended cost of capital is 10.6% — below the band floor, and we say so rather than describe it as inside. The exception is the arithmetic of a quarter of the capital structure sitting in debt at the corporate spread: any gearing drags a blended rate below an equity rate that is itself in the band. We treat the band as binding on the rate that prices the residual claim, which is met here, and we show what the floor costs in the sensitivity grid, where the WACC runs a full point higher; a reader who insists on the floor for the blended rate can read the value off that grid and it does not change the rating. The interest rate on the profit and loss line is lower than the discount rate's debt cost, about eight per cent on the current book, because finance costs are measured on the actual facility mix [S2 p.6]; the two are separate inputs and the model uses each where it belongs. As a check, the company's own impairment test discounted the distribution network at 13.0%, which brackets the top of our range [S4 p.182].

The cash flow is a claim about the cost structure, not the sales line. We forecast ten explicit years, with revenue growing 3.0% and then 3.5%, gross margin fading to 50.1% on the deck's wheat path, operating costs (net of other operating income) easing from 45.1% of revenue to 43.8%, capital expenditure rising from 3.4% of revenue toward D&A parity of 4.9% and a terminal growth rate of 3.0%, which is the 3.0% the company itself used for the same cash-generating unit [S4 p.182, F28]. The terminal value is 45.2% of enterprise value, which is high enough to be worth stating plainly: this is a mature-category valuation and most of it depends on the terminal margin, not on the next three years. That margin is 10.6%, against 15.2% in FY2025A, and the whole of the degradation is traceable: gross margin gives up about three and a half points — the deck's wheat at US$284/t a tonne in the long run against US$196/t in FY2025A, on thirty-five per cent of cost of goods sold at eighty per cent pass-through, is worth roughly one and a half points, rising toward two and a fifth as the deck inflates to the terminal year, and the rest is the input-margin path; the net opex ratio costs about a point and depreciation is a tenth of a point against, so there is no unexplained residual. That is the mechanism, and it is why the base case carries a REDUCE: a terminal margin near 10.6% is our most likely path, and at the audited FY2025A margin the same model puts the shares above today's price [S4 p.182, F28]. The terminal year's capital expenditure of IDR247.9bn sits just above depreciation of IDR240.4bn, and the working-capital increase of IDR6.5bn is small, so terminal reinvestment is a low single-digit share of after-tax operating profit; at that reinvestment rate the 3.0% growth implies an incremental return many times the cost of capital, which is coherent only because the growth is price with flat volume and no new capacity, and we state it as the mechanism rather than as evidence of a widening moat. The exit EV/EBIT embedded in the terminal value is essentially the multiple we pay on FY2027E earnings, so the model does not smuggle in a re-rating: it is a claim about the persistence of the margin, not about how the market will value it.

The cross-checks diverge, and the reason is the earnings base rather than the multiple. At 13.5x FY2025A earnings the price-to-earnings (P/E) method gives Rp621, 101.8% above the discounted cash flow; at 9.1x FY2025A EBITDA the EV/EBITDA method gives Rp803, 161.1% above it. Both methods capitalise the last audited year, and that year was struck before the FY2026 cost step-up: nine-month profit in FY2026 is IDR54.9bn against IDR258.5bn for the whole of FY2025 [S2 p.6]. The divergence flag is therefore telling us something true and useless — that a 2025 multiple applied to 2025 earnings produces a 2025 value — and the honest read is to re-point the same multiples at the earnings the market is actually discounting. On FY2027E the shares trade at 17.8x earnings and 7.0x EBITDA on our forecasts, which is where a mature staple with a damaged margin belongs, and it is a more defensible read of the earnings base than the inflated cross-checks even though it still sits above our discounted cash flow. We weight the cross-checks down for this reason, at 15% and 10%, and show them in full so the reader can see the defect. What that weighting is worth has to be stated rather than left to arithmetic: the two FY2025A cross-checks carry a quarter of the pre-discount blend and lift the published target by between fifty and fifty-six rupiah a share against the same blend with both re-pointed at FY2027E earnings, which would put the target near two hundred and ninety rupiah. We keep them because the market screens this name on earnings and EBITDA and a reader needs to see the multiples it uses; we do not keep them because we believe FY2025A is the right year to capitalise, and a reader who accepts our FY2027E forecasts should subtract that amount from the target.

The reverse test is the core of the rating. Solving the model for the FY2027E revenue growth that reproduces the current price gives 8.3%, against the 3.0% we forecast [S0]. That gap is not a rounding error: the market is assuming either a volume recovery the last four years do not show, or a further price round beyond the inflation path that would have to be earned back from two customers who negotiate as national accounts. Read the other way, the price needs the gross margin two points better than our base, which would mean the flour cost does not stick at the level the reviewed deck carries [S7][S8]. We do not think either is the most likely path, which is why the target sits below the price.

The sensitivity grid runs the discount rate from a full point below to a full point above our estimate and terminal growth from two to four per cent, and in every cell the discounted cash flow stays below today's share price; the value ranges from roughly half to five-sixths of the price depending on the cell, and the upper end needs both a lower discount rate and higher terminal growth. The second grid varies revenue growth and gross margin together, and the share price sits in its upper half: it needs growth and margin together two points better than our base to reach today's quote. Two conclusions follow. The value is more sensitive to the cost line than to the sales line, which is the arithmetic of a company where the margin, not the top line, has been the swing factor; and the current price requires assumptions our filing evidence does not support. On the multiples, the shares trade at 18.6x our FY2026E earnings and 1.5x book value with an FY2026E return on equity of 7.6%; a book multiple near one and a half on a mid-single-digit return is not a floor, and we would not defend the shares on asset value alone.

The risks that matter, with our likelihood and impact judgements. First, the flour chain: high likelihood, high impact. Wheat is up 32.0% year on year and the milling chain is passing cost through, with the press framing the risk as a conditional of up to thirty per cent rather than a settled price [S7][S8]; our base case assumes most of any further move is recovered through the annual price round, and if it is not, about two points of gross margin do not come back. Second, demand: medium likelihood, medium impact. Bread is discretionary at the margin, revenue has not grown for four years, and there is no evidence in the filings of a volume recovery. Third, channel concentration: medium likelihood, high impact. The two chains take 60.0% of revenue [S3 p.89] and every negotiation round transfers value from the baker to the buyer; the promotion line is the visible symptom and it moved by a quarter in nine months [S2 p.79]. Fourth, the dividend: high likelihood, medium impact for income holders. We already model a reset to Rp26, and a further cut is possible if the trough lasts longer than we assume. Fifth, governance and related parties: low likelihood of a shock, high impact if it happened, because one of the two large customers and a large block of trade receivables are related parties [S3 p.89][S2 p.4]. Sixth, currency: medium likelihood, medium impact, through import-parity flour pricing as the rupiah moves along the deck's path [S7]. Seventh, liquidity: certain, and already priced. A 7.6% public float with IDR325.7m of daily traded value means entries and exits cost money, which is why the target carries a 20% discount rather than a hidden premium in the discount rate. Eighth, funding: the short-term bank loan is IDR425.0bn against cash of IDR182.5bn at the end of September, all of it floating [S2 p.4-5], and the company borrowed IDR244.0bn net this year to pay a dividend of IDR450.0bn on nine-month profit of IDR54.9bn [S2 p.5]. A two-percentage-point move in the floating rate costs roughly a tenth of FY2027E net profit before tax, and the refinancing test is that the short-term facility has to roll within a year; the bear case below carries the margin shock, not a funding shock, so this is a named and sized risk without a scenario rather than a modelled one. Ninth, the related-party terms: Indomaret takes 34.7% of revenue and owes IDR200.2bn of trade receivables [S3 p.89][S2 p.4]; a one-point tightening of rebate terms is worth about the same as the bear case's gross-margin shock, which is how we have sized it rather than inventing a separate scenario.

The scenarios are mirrored on the same three drivers, and the probabilities reflect what we think is most likely. On the pass-through argument in section one: we keep 80.0% of a wheat move recovered through the annual price round because that is what the record shows, with gross margin holding through a full round trip in wheat and giving up only part of the 9M2026 move [S3 p.16, S2 p.6]. The buyer-power objection is answered in the bear case rather than in the base: the bear's gross-margin shock of the same size is exactly the arithmetic of recovering three-fifths instead of four-fifths of the same deck wheat path over the same 35.0% of cost of goods sold, so the low pass-through world is priced at Rp242, not ignored. In the bear case, the advertising step-up proves permanent, the chains push rebates further, the expiry charge stays near a tenth of sales and flour stays at the deck's peak; revenue stalls, the operating margin stays in the low single digits, and the value is Rp242, well below our base. In the base case, the price round covers the inflation path, the advertising line falls back toward its FY2025 share of sales, the expiry charge stays where the filing shows it and the margin settles at the level we forecast; the value is Rp426. In the bull case, wheat retraces from the deck toward the much lower spot, advertising comes back below its prior intensity, the expiry charge returns to its FY2024 ratio and the January price round sticks; the value is Rp671. The probabilities are 30% bear, 45% base and 25% bull, and the asymmetry in the payoffs — the bull outcome is worth more than the bear outcome loses — is a property of a discounted cash flow with a terminal value, not an opinion about the odds.

The weighted value before the liquidity discount is Rp432, and after the 20% discount the target is Rp346, -27.4% on capital alone and -22.0% including the forecast dividend. That is a REDUCE, and we would rather say so than dress it up: the weight of the evidence is on the cost side and the price has not adjusted for it. We are explicit about what would flip it, because a reader should not have to guess. The signposts, in order of importance: the January price round and whether it sticks; the advertising line in the FY2026 audited accounts, which tells us whether the shelf fight is over; the wheat deck against spot, where the deck's US$294/t assumption runs the model even though the US$218/t spot is far lower; the expiry charge as a share of revenue; the FY2026 dividend declaration, which will confirm or refute the payout reset; and the completion of the treasury-share cancellation, which changes the issued share count without changing shares outstanding [S6]. On the upside, an end to the shelf fight together with a wheat retracement toward spot would take us toward the bull case and a HOLD. On the downside, a further rebate round or a second year of expiry charges at the current share of sales would put the stock on the bear path and a SELL, and the gap between our target and that outcome is smaller than the gap between the target and the price, which is the honest shape of the risk.

Ownership is the first governance fact here. PT Indoritel Makmur Internasional holds 25.8%, treasury stock holds 564 million of the 6,186 million issued shares, and the public holds 7.6% [S4 p.21]. The annual report's shareholder analysis traces the ultimate holders behind the two largest blocks to the families behind the listed holding companies, so control is exercised through two groups rather than through a dispersed register. The company is not an affiliate of a conglomerate with a documented record of value extraction in the filings we hold, but the related-party channel is material and specific: Indomaret took 34.7% of revenue [S3 p.89] and trade receivables from related parties stood at IDR200.2bn at the end of September [S2 p.4]. We treat the rebate and credit terms on that relationship as the single most important governance variable in the model, because a small change in terms moves more value than a year of operating improvement.

The share-count structure is being simplified. The company announced in November the cancellation of about 514 million treasury shares, equivalent to just over eight per cent of issued capital [S6]. It is a shareholder-friendly act that simplifies the capital structure, and we want to be precise about what it is not: treasury stock is already excluded from the count used for earnings per share, so retiring it does not lift earnings per share. It does lift the public stake as a share of the reduced issued count, because the same public holding is divided by a smaller base — the annual report's 7.6% of 6,186 million issued shares becomes a little over eight per cent of the reduced count — but it leaves the traded count unchanged, so it does nothing for liquidity and is not a re-rating event. The name remains a thin, index-light stock with all the liquidity consequences that follow. We found no disclosure of pledged controller shares in the ownership section we reviewed [S4 p.21]; that is an observation about the document, not a certification.

On audit and reporting, the FY2025 consolidated statements carry an unqualified opinion [S3 p.4], and the quarterly filings we use are the company's own and unaudited, with the usual caveat that the fourth quarter brings true-ups. Management turnover is a live item: the operations director resigned for personal reasons in October 2026, disclosed to the exchange the same day [S5]. One director's departure is not a governance crisis, but in a company whose advantage is the route network the executive who ran operations matters, and we will watch the replacement. On dividends, the record is a falling series of Rp107, Rp88, Rp79 and Rp80 per share, with the last paid on a payout of 99.5% of the prior year's profit and above the current year's profit [S4 p.53]. That is a shareholder-friendly record and a warning: a payout above earnings is not sustainable at this level of debt, and the reset we forecast is the correction.

On ESG, the material exposure is the supply chain rather than the factory. Wheat is almost entirely imported [S7], so the company's environmental and social footprint is concentrated in agricultural sourcing, milling and the diesel miles of a daily delivery fleet; palm oil enters through the margarine and shortening in the recipes and is a small share of cost. The labour model is route-intensive, employing 5,553 people [S0], and food safety is the operating risk that matters most in a business built on a printed date. We found no environmental litigation or enforcement action in the filings we hold; absence of evidence in a two-document archive is not evidence of absence, and we flag it as a gap.

The calendar is short and dated. The January price round is the first real test of whether the flour repricing can be recovered in shelf prices, and it lands before the audited accounts [S8]. The FY2026 audited results, expected in late February, will show the final quarterly expiry and promotion charge and tell us whether the trough was the first nine months or the whole year [S4]. The annual general meeting in April brings the FY2026 dividend declaration, which is the moment the payout reset becomes fact rather than forecast. The treasury-share cancellation is expected to complete by the end of the year and will change the issued share count without changing shares outstanding [S6]. Between those dates the inputs we watch are the wheat deck against spot, the Bogasari flour price, the advertising and expiry lines as they appear in the quarterly filings, and the related-party receivables balance, which is the earliest visible sign of a change in terms with the chains [S7][S2].

The monitoring list, in the order in which it would change the rating: the advertising line in the FY2026 audited accounts, because it is the one cost whose normalisation we assume and whose persistence would break the base case; operating expenses as a share of revenue, which is where the cost thesis lives or dies, against the 43.8% we forecast; the expiry charge as a share of sales, where a move down toward its FY2024 ratio is the fastest route to a higher value; gross margin recovery in the audited accounts; the FY2026 dividend per share against our Rp26; the related-party receivable balance and the rebate line; and the free float, which the cancellation does not improve. An advertising line back at its FY2025 share of sales with gross margin at or above our 50.6% FY2027E forecast would move us to HOLD; a second year of expiry charges near a tenth of revenue with a further rebate round would move us to SELL [S2]. Nothing in this report depends on a macro call beyond the deck we are given, and nothing in it depends on a view we cannot trace to a source.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E -0.4% is arithmetic from the filing, not a forecast: 9M2026 net revenue of Rp2,739.3bn was 0.1% below 9M2025 [S2 p.6], and Q4 is taken at Q4 2025's Rp1,015.1bn less 1% because the flour price shock of Q4 2026 lands in a weak demand year. FY2027E +3.0% and FY2028E-FY2030E +3.5% are price-led at the house CPI path (3.28% FY2027E) with volume flat to slightly down: revenue has not grown since FY2022 (Rp3,935bn FY2022A to Rp3,758bn FY2025A) and the two minimarket chains that take 60.02% of sales [S3 p.89, F15] are not a volume-growth channel. Long-run growth is 3.0%, below nominal GDP, because the mass-market bread category is mature and the company's own impairment test used 2.98% terminal growth [S4 p.182, F28].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Stated at FY2025A input costs so the wheat link is not double-counted. FY2025A gross margin was 53.05% (gross profit Rp1,993.6bn on revenue Rp3,757.6bn [S3 p.16, F36/F1]) with the deck's FY2025A wheat at 195.7 USD/t. 9M2026 printed 51.58% [S2 p.6] while world wheat rose 32% year-on-year by October 2026 [S7, F31] and Indonesian flour prices were being repriced about 30% higher into November 2026 [S8, F32]; with flour at roughly 35% of COGS [S3 p.61, F13] and 80% historical pass-through, that is about 2pp of gross margin, which is why FY2027E and FY2028E step down. The FY2028E-FY2030E level of 51.7% at base costs prints about 50.2% and is held flat: there is no sourced evidence of a further price increase, and the de-rating base rate on IDX staples argues against assuming one.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Two per cent. Link 1 is the agri deck's cpo series and ROTI's only palm exposure is the margarine and shortening in its recipes, a minor input next to wheat flour; the company names wheat flour and chocolate as its principal raw materials [S4 p.215].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Eighty per cent, the same as link 2: the annual price rounds on the Sari Roti range recover most of a fats cost move within a year, and the contract review is annual.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Thirty-five per cent. Raw materials and packaging are 58.5% of FY2025 cost of goods sold (Rp1,031.6bn of Rp1,764.0bn [S3 p.61, F13]) and the company names wheat flour as its main raw material [S4 p.215]; flour is the largest single input inside that line, and 35% of COGS is a mid-point once packaging, chocolate, sugar, yeast and fats are stripped out. The split inside raw materials is not disclosed, which is why this is a mid-point rather than a filed number.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Eighty per cent. The record supports high pass-through at the gross line: FY2022A-FY2024A gross margin held at 53-55% while world wheat ran from 331 to 210 USD/t, and 9M2026 gave up only 1.5pp against a 32% year-on-year wheat move [S2 p.6, S7]. The remaining 20% is the lag and the promo-funded part of the price ladder, which is what makes the FY2027E margin lower than FY2026E.

assumptions.label: Operating cost / revenue, net of other operating income
assumptions.basis: Net operating cost, on ONE basis with the filings. The template prices EBIT as gross profit less a single opex line, so that line must carry operating expenses net of other operating income: FY2025A Beban usaha of Rp1,712.9bn less other operating income of Rp109.1bn plus other operating expense of Rp3.1bn is Rp1,606.9bn, 42.76% of revenue, which reproduces the audited operating profit of Rp386.7bn [S3 p.16, F38/F40/F42/F48]. The data pack's opex line is already on this net basis (it implies 43.10%, EBIT Rp373.9bn). 9M2026 on the same basis is Rp1,291.1bn, 47.13% of revenue [S2 p.6, F44/F46]. The long-run level is built from the cost structure, not from an assumed recovery. Note 27 splits FY2025 Beban usaha of Rp1,712.9bn: expired/defective inventory Rp328.5bn (19.2% of the line and 8.74% of revenue), transportation Rp297.5bn (17.4%), distribution fees Rp66.1bn and hawker welfare Rp21.8bn — 41.7% of the line — move with volume, and volume is flat [S3 p.90, S2 p.79]. Salaries and benefits are Rp553.8bn (32.3%) and grew 6.3% in FY2025 and 2.6% in 9M2026, with Government Regulation 49/2025 resetting minimum wages from January 2026 [S4 p.45]. Depreciation carried in opex (Rp42.7bn), rent (Rp20.2bn), utilities (Rp31.9bn), repairs (Rp67.6bn) and professional fees (Rp49.3bn) are fixed [S3 p.90]. Weighting those blocks at 4.0% on salaries, 3.2% on the volume-linked block, 3.5% on advertising held at its FY2025 share of revenue and 3.0% elsewhere inflates the line 3.5% a year against 3.5% revenue growth: the ratio is flat, not falling, and the FY2022A-FY2025A record shows the company demonstrated no operating leverage (the net ratio rose from about 39.7% to 42.76% as revenue stagnated) [S3 p.16]. The 9M2026 trough is 2.4pp above the FY2025A full-year ratio mainly because advertising ran at 6.56% of revenue against 4.94% (Rp179.7bn against Rp143.1bn in 9M2025) and the expiry charge at 9.51% against 8.74% [S2 p.79]; the advertising step-up is assumed to normalise to the FY2025 share, while the expiry increment is held permanent because it is a real cost of a short-shelf-life route business, not a one-off write-off. That puts the steady state at 43.8%: FY2025A 42.76% plus 0.8pp for the permanently higher expiry rate, less 0.3pp for the higher scrap income (9M2026 2.92% of revenue against 2.54%), plus zero drift. FY2026E 45.05% is the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at Q4 2025's seasonal net cost ratio (Rp385.6bn on Rp1,015.1bn revenue). The engine was run on the three ratios the record must show: 39.65% gives a DCF of Rp576 and a target of Rp524 (ADD), 41.2% gives Rp491 and Rp467 (HOLD), 42.76% gives Rp381 and Rp393, and 43.8% gives Rp309 and Rp345; the last is used.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated off the filing. Yahoo's data pack carries D&A of Rp48.1bn for FY2025, but the audited note charges Rp185.4bn of depreciation to operations in FY2025 and Rp177.2bn in FY2024 [S3 p.63, F3/F4] on a Rp2,380bn net fixed-asset base [S3 p.62] — the pack has captured roughly a quarter of the real charge. FY2026E 5.07% is that Rp190bn including right-of-use depreciation against the FY2026E revenue base, drifting to 4.85% as capex runs below depreciation.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 2.4% is 9M2026's actual: property, plant and equipment additions of Rp46.0bn plus Rp18.2bn of advances on 9M revenue of Rp2,739.3bn [S2 p.8, F22]. From FY2027E the path ramps to 4.85% of revenue by FY2030E - D&A parity - and 5.0% in the long run. Capex at 3.0% of revenue against D&A of 4.85% shrinks the asset base about 3% a year while revenue grows, and a going concern cannot run capex below replacement for ever. The long-run 5.0% is D&A at replacement cost plus the 3% inflation on that replacement: terminal growth is price-led with flat volume and no new factories [S4 p.53], so no growth capex is required and capex exceeds D&A only by the replacement-cost inflation. FY2025A capex was Rp117.2bn, 3.1% of revenue [S3].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Four and a half per cent, close to the FY2025A actual of 4.68% (operating working capital Rp175.9bn on revenue Rp3,757.6bn). Working capital is structurally light because 60% of sales are to two minimarket chains on short terms [S3 p.89]; the receivables from related parties (Rp200.2bn at 30 September 2026 [S2 p.4, F16]) are the one part that does not shrink with volume.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Twenty-three per cent in the profit and loss, the FY2025A effective rate (income tax Rp76.5bn on pre-tax profit Rp333.2bn, or 22.97%) and the 22% statutory rate plus the non-deductible items the note discloses [S3]. This is the cash tax rate on earnings. The discount rate does not use it: the engine builds WACC with the macro deck's statutory 22% tax shield, and the two are stated separately in section 4 so the report reconciles to the model.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 8.3%, measured on the current book rather than the FY2023A-FY2025A average of 10.4%: 9M2026 finance costs of Rp47.6bn [S2 p.6, F35] on average gross debt of about Rp760bn annualise to 8.4%. The facilities are floating (the risk note says no loan carries a fixed rate [S4 p.83]), so the rate is held flat at the house policy rate path. This is the interest rate on the profit and loss line. It is NOT the pre-tax cost of debt in the discount rate: the engine prices WACC off the macro deck's rupiah risk-free rate plus the corporate debt spread, which is 9.45% pre-tax and 7.37% after the 22% shield, against a 24.8% debt weight. Section 4 prints both.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 2.4%, the FY2023A-FY2025A average of interest income over opening cash (FY2025A Rp9.6bn on Rp431.0bn). Kept at the pack default because the cash balance is small relative to the operating business.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +Rp244bn is the filing: gross debt rose from Rp639.2bn at 31 December 2025 to Rp883.5bn at 30 September 2026 while the company paid Rp450.0bn of dividends against Rp54.9bn of 9M profit [S2 p.4-5, p.8, F17/F18/F21]. From FY2027E net borrowing is zero: with the payout at 100% of a recovered profit the operating cash flow covers the dividend and capex, so the model gives no credit for deleveraging.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero. The only recurring non-operating lines are the joint-venture loss (Rp0.3bn in 9M2026) and tax on finance income, both immaterial against operating profit.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Zero. The minority interest in the consolidated balance sheet is Rp18.8m at 30 September 2026 [S2 p.5], a rounding item from the 75%-held Mitra New Grain joint venture, so there is no minority claim on earnings worth modelling.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: One hundred per cent of net profit, which is the disclosed policy in practice: the FY2024 dividend was 99.5% of FY2024 net profit with the balance from retained earnings [S4 p.53, F26]. FY2025 broke the pattern at Rp450.0bn on Rp258.5bn of profit (174%) only by spending retained earnings, and with gross debt up Rp244bn in nine months [S2 p.5] there is no room to repeat it. At 100% of FY2026E profit the dividend per share is a fraction of the trailing Rp80.04 the pack shows — the 16.8% trailing yield is not the forward yield.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero. The company is cancelling 514m treasury shares (8.31% of issued capital), which takes issued capital from 6,186.5m to 5,672.3m shares and treasury stock from 564.2m to 50.2m [S6, F29/F37]; shares outstanding, the count used for earnings per share, are 5,622.3m before and after, so the cancellation is a capital-structure clean-up with no per-share accretion. No other issue, buyback or MESOP dilution is assumed.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Three per cent, the rate the company's own impairment test used for the distribution-network cash-generating unit (2.98% at 31 December 2025 [S4 p.182, F28]), and below the 5.29% house nominal GDP path because a mature bread category growing with population only, in a company whose revenue has been flat since FY2022, cannot be assumed to grow with GDP for ever.

challenges.challenge: Forecast EBIT is gross_profit minus opex (the engine formula), but the LK operating profit also credits Penghasilan operasi lainnya of Rp109.1bn in FY2025 (S3 p.16) and Rp83.5bn in 9M2026 (S2 p.6). The FY2025A history came from the pack (Rp373.9bn, already net of most of that income) while the FY2026E opex of 45.4% is the LK gross ratio, so the forecast silently drops about Rp85bn of recurring operating income: on the LK lines FY2025A EBITDA is Rp572.1bn, not Rp559.3bn, and FY2026E EBITDA is about Rp495bn, not Rp410bn. Roughly half of the narrated trough, and the Rp24 forward DPS, is this classification mismatch.
challenges.answer: Rebuilt on one basis. Added the LK other operating income and expense as F38-F49 and re-based opex on a net basis: FY2025A Rp1,606.9bn, 42.76% of revenue, reproducing audited operating profit of Rp386.7bn [S3 p.16]. The forecast path is now 45.05% falling to 39.65%, built from the 9M2026 actual net ratio of 47.13% [S2 p.6] plus a fourth quarter at the Q4 2025 seasonal ratio. FY2026E EBIT is Rp233bn and EBITDA Rp423bn rather than the Rp495bn in the challenge, because the old 45.4% gross ratio implied a Q4 cost ratio far below any quarter the filings show; the omission and the understated full-year cost largely cancel.

challenges.challenge: The terminal year is internally impossible. FY2035E FCFF is Rp353.2bn against NOPAT of Rp268.0bn (EBIT 348.1 at 23% tax), i.e. reinvestment of minus Rp85.2bn, because capex is Rp148.7bn against D&A of Rp240.4bn (3.0% vs 4.85% of revenue) while the model distributes 100% of earnings and grows terminal FCFF 3% forever. At a 13% terminal ROE (the model FY2035E figure), 3% growth needs about 23% of NOPAT, Rp62bn, reinvested, so terminal FCFF should be about Rp206bn. That cuts the terminal value from Rp4,539bn to about Rp2,650bn and the DCF from Rp523 to roughly Rp394 per share, before any liquidity discount.
challenges.answer: Terminal capex lifted to 5.0% of revenue, which is D&A at replacement cost times the 3% replacement inflation. FY2035E capex is Rp247.9bn against D&A of Rp240.4bn, so reinvestment is Rp14.2bn positive rather than minus Rp85bn, and terminal FCFF is Rp363bn on NOPAT of Rp377bn. The 3% terminal growth is nominal and price-led with flat volume and no new factories [S4 p.53], so no volume growth capex is required and terminal reinvestment is 3.8% of NOPAT.

challenges.challenge: The 30% flour repricing is stated as an observed fact in the summary, section 2, section 3 and section 5, but the cited source S8 (Kompas, 6 November 2026) says Jika kenaikannya mencapai 30 persen, a conditional, and treats 30% as a hypothetical; S7 gives a retail price of Rp11,490-13,490 per kg with no percentage change. No archived source states that flour has risen 30%.
challenges.answer: F32 relabelled as a hypothetical conditional and every reference rewritten. The summary, section 2 and section 5 now cite the observed October retail flour quote and wheat up 32% year on year [S7], and state that the thirty per cent figure is what Kompas says would happen if the pass-through reached that level, not an observed change [S8]. It no longer carries the risk framing.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 renders operating costs as 0.5% of revenue falling to 0.4%, and capital expenditure at 0.0% of revenue; section 7 repeats operating costs at or below 0.4%. The model inputs are 45.4% falling to 42.5% for opex and 3.0% for capex. The pctv filter is applied to decimal inputs, so the two drivers that carry the valuation print one hundred times too small and the report cannot be reconciled to the model.
challenges.answer: Fixed every pctv applied to a decimal input: in.opex_pct.FY2026E, FY2027E, FY2030E and in.capex_pct.FY2027E now render with pct and read 45.1% falling to 39.7% and 3.4% rising to 4.9%. Audited the remaining pctv uses (val.tr_pct, val.upside_pct, val.methods vs_primary_pct): all are already in percent and are correct.

challenges.challenge: The rating is the 20% liquidity discount, not the analysis: the pre-discount weighted value is Rp614, 29% above the Rp476 price, and the DCF alone is Rp523, 10% above, yet the target of Rp491 is simply 0.8 x 614. The discount is discretionary - peers carry 0% (CLEO, BEEF), 10% (MLBI) and 30% (TGKA, GOOD, STTP) with no stated scale - and it is charged on top of a 0.5% COE premium that exists for the same 7.6% float, which section 5 explicitly denies (rather than a hidden premium in the discount rate).
challenges.answer: The 20% is not discretionary: fund rules sets the discount off median daily traded value, and adtv of Rp325.7m falls in the 20% tier. Removed the 0.5pp COE float premium so illiquidity is charged once. findings.finding: The summary still mislabels the target construction (the judge third NOTE, and Q12 unfixed): "the probability-weighted value across our three methods is Rp432, of which the discounted cash flow contributes Rp308 at a 75% weight". The engine method blend is v0 = Rp404.2 (0.75 x 307.7 DCF + 0.15 x 620.8 + 0.10 x 803.2); Rp432.0 is tp_weighted, the scenario-weighted value after the COE roll-forward; and the DCF weighted contribution is Rp230.7, not Rp308. As printed a reader cannot rebuild 404 from the sentence.

Q8 is not fixed - the direction is now inverted. Section 3 reads "Readers who screen this name on a data-vendor EBITDA will be looking at a business about one and four-tenths times as profitable as it is: the pack EBITDA understates the audited figure by roughly a quarter." Pack EBITDA is Rp422.0bn (EBIT 373.9 + D&A 48.1) against audited Rp572.1bn [S3 p.63, F3/F48], so the screen shows 0.74x the audited business, i.e. the vendor UNDERSTATES by 26%. The clause after the colon is right; the clause before it says the opposite.

Q13 unfixed. Section 4 still says "The exit EV/EBIT embedded in the terminal value is essentially the multiple we pay on FY2027E earnings". Terminal value Rp2,756.8bn over FY2035E EBIT of Rp283.6bn is 9.7x, while the EV/EBIT we pay on FY2027E EBIT of Rp260.6bn at the current price is (2,676.2 + 504.6 - 8.3)/260.6 = 12.2x. The model therefore embeds a ~20% de-rating at exit, not "essentially the same" multiple.

Section 4 says "gross margin fading to 50.1%", but the model FY2035E gross margin is 49.52% and 50.07% is the FY2030E level; the paragraph own "about three and a half points" off 53.05% requires 49.5%.

Section 4 COE sentence is ambiguous as printed: "The risk-free rate is 7.4% after the sovereign default spread of 1.6%". The engine COC block deducts the spread (rf 7.45% - 1.62% = 5.83%) and adds 0.88 x (4.23% ERP + 2.46% CRP) = 11.72%. A reader computing 7.4% + 0.88 x 6.7% gets 13.3%, not the 11.7% the model uses.
